questions.stem:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

"The gullies that now scar the hills of Anambra were once shallow footpaths. Year after year, farmers cleared the slopes for cassava, and year after year the rains carried away what the roots had held. By the time the community petitioned the state government, whole compounds had slid into the ravine."

According to the passage, what turned the footpaths into gullies?

options.text: The state government's delay in responding to the petition
The clearing of the slopes, which left no roots to hold the soil against the rains
The building of compounds too close to the edge of the ravine
An unusually heavy rainy season in a single year

questions.explanation: The passage states the cause directly: the farmers cleared the slopes and "the rains carried away what the roots had held". Removing the vegetation removed the roots that bound the soil, so the rain could wash it away. The phrase *year after year*, repeated twice, shows the damage was cumulative.

distractorRationale.a: The petition is mentioned only as a later event; the passage does not say the delay caused the gullies
distractorRationale.c: The compounds are described as victims that slid into the ravine, not as a cause
distractorRationale.d: The repetition of *year after year* rules out a single exceptional season

questions.stem:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

"The engineers who came spoke of check dams and terracing; the elders spoke of a land that had been punished for impatience."

What does the expression *a land that had been punished for impatience* mean as used here?

options.text: The soil had lost its fertility because the rains came too early each year
The land had been ruined because people had farmed it hastily without letting it recover
The community had been fined by the government for damaging the environment
The elders believed the engineers had arrived too late to help

questions.explanation: The elders are contrasted with the engineers: where the engineers name technical remedies, the elders offer a moral reading of the same damage. *Impatience* refers to the farmers' repeated clearing of the slopes without allowing the land to rest, and *punished* presents the erosion as the consequence.

distractorRationale.a: Reads *impatience* as a property of the rain rather than of the people
distractorRationale.c: Takes *punished* literally as a legal penalty, which the passage never mentions
distractorRationale.d: Confuses the elders' explanation of the cause with a complaint about timing

questions.stem:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

"The gullies that now scar the hills of Anambra were once shallow footpaths... By the time the community petitioned the state government, whole compounds had slid into the ravine."

What does the phrase *by the time* suggest about the community's petition?

options.text: The petition was well organised and promptly submitted
The petition came only after serious damage had already been done
The petition was rejected by the state government
The petition was written by the elders rather than the farmers

questions.explanation: *By the time* marks one event as already complete when another happens, so the loss of the compounds had occurred before the petition was written. The writer uses the phrase to imply that the community acted too late, without ever saying so directly.

distractorRationale.a: The construction implies delay, which is the opposite of promptness
distractorRationale.c: The passage says nothing at all about the government's response
distractorRationale.d: The elders are mentioned elsewhere in the passage, but not as the authors of the petition

questions.stem:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

"Mama Nkechi had sold tomatoes at the same corner for thirty-one years. When the new market was built with concrete stalls and a locked gate, she was allocated a space at the back, where no passer-by would ever see her. Within four months she had returned to the roadside."

Why did Mama Nkechi return to the roadside?

options.text: Because the rent for the concrete stall was too high for her
Because her new stall was hidden from passing customers
Because the market gate was locked before she finished trading
Because she had traded on the roadside for thirty-one years and preferred the habit

questions.explanation: The passage says her space was at the back "where no passer-by would ever see her", and a trader with no passing customers has no trade. Everything else in the extract — the locked gate, the concrete, the thirty-one years — is background detail rather than the stated reason.

distractorRationale.a: Rent is never mentioned in the extract
distractorRationale.c: The locked gate describes the new market's design but is not given as her reason for leaving
distractorRationale.d: Habit is a plausible guess, but the passage supplies a commercial reason instead

questions.stem:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

"Within four months she had returned to the roadside, paying a daily levy to a man whose authority nobody could explain."

What does the writer imply about the man collecting the levy?

options.text: He was a senior official of the new market management
He had no legitimate right to collect the money
He collected the levy on behalf of the traders' association
He was well known and respected by all the roadside traders

questions.explanation: The clause *whose authority nobody could explain* is a quiet way of saying that no one could point to any legal basis for his demands. The writer never calls him an extortionist, but the wording invites the reader to draw that conclusion — which is exactly what an inference question tests.

distractorRationale.a: An official's authority would be easy to explain, so this contradicts the clause
distractorRationale.c: No association is mentioned anywhere in the extract
distractorRationale.d: Being unable to explain his authority undercuts, rather than supports, respect

questions.stem:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

"Mama Nkechi knew which customers would haggle and which would pay without a word, and she priced accordingly."

What does *she priced accordingly* mean in this context?

options.text: She charged every customer the same fixed price
She set her opening price to suit the customer she was facing
She reduced her prices whenever business was slow
She followed the prices agreed by the other traders

questions.explanation: *Accordingly* means 'in a way that matches what has just been described', and what precedes it is her knowledge of who would haggle. So she quoted a higher opening price to bargainers and a straight price to those who would not argue. The word depends entirely on the clause before it.

distractorRationale.a: A single fixed price would make her knowledge of hagglers useless
distractorRationale.c: Slow business is not mentioned; the passage links her pricing to customers, not to trade volume
distractorRationale.d: Other traders' prices are not referred to anywhere in the extract

questions.stem:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

"Examinations, we are told, measure ability. In practice they measure a narrower thing: the capacity to recall, under pressure, what has recently been rehearsed. The candidate who reads widely but slowly is punished; the candidate who memorises a hundred likely questions is rewarded."

What is the writer's main argument?

options.text: Examinations are unnecessary and should be abolished
Examinations test memorisation rather than the broad ability they claim to measure
Candidates should stop reading widely and concentrate on likely questions
Slow readers are naturally less able than fast readers

questions.explanation: The writer sets up a contrast between the claim — that examinations measure ability — and the practice, which rewards recent rehearsal. The phrase *a narrower thing* is the hinge of the argument. Nothing in the extract calls for abolition; the complaint is about what is being measured.

distractorRationale.a: Overstates the argument; criticising what examinations measure is not the same as rejecting them
distractorRationale.c: Describes the behaviour the writer deplores, not the advice being given
distractorRationale.d: The writer says slow readers are *punished* by the system, which implies the system is at fault

questions.stem:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

"Examinations, we are told, measure ability. In practice they measure a narrower thing... Until the questions themselves change, no amount of exhortation will change how students read."

What is the writer's tone in this passage?
questions.explanation: The phrases *we are told* and *in practice* signal scepticism about the official claim, so the tone is critical. But the writer builds a case rather than complaining — the final sentence offers a condition for change — so the criticism is reasoned rather than angry.

distractorRationale.a: Nothing in the extract praises examinations
distractorRationale.c: There is no joke, exaggeration or playfulness anywhere in the passage
distractorRationale.d: A detached writer would not use loaded words such as *punished* and *rewarded*

questions.stem:
Read the extract and answer the question that follows.

"The candidate who reads widely but slowly is punished; the candidate who memorises a hundred likely questions is rewarded."

In what sense is the wide reader *punished*?

options.text: He is disqualified from sitting the examination
He scores less than a memoriser even though his understanding may be deeper
He is criticised by his teachers for reading irrelevant books
He is forced to write more than the other candidates

questions.explanation: *Punished* is used figuratively. The writer's point is that the marking system gives lower rewards to the wide reader than to the memoriser, so the penalty is a loss of marks rather than any formal sanction. The parallel word *rewarded* in the same sentence confirms that both terms refer to examination outcomes.

distractorRationale.a: Reads the word literally as a formal penalty, which the passage does not describe
distractorRationale.c: Teachers' opinions are not mentioned in the extract
distractorRationale.d: Length of answers is not the subject of the sentence

questions.stem: In a comprehension test, an answer that is factually true about the world but not supported by the passage should still be accepted.
questions.explanation: False. Comprehension measures how well you have read the passage, so every answer must be traceable to something the writer stated or clearly implied. Examiners deliberately include options that are plausible in real life but absent from the text, and candidates who answer from general knowledge lose the mark.

questions.stem: In the passage, the author describes the effects of climate change on the local farming community. What is the primary tone of the author?
questions.explanation: The author's tone is pessimistic as it reflects concern and hopelessness regarding the negative impacts of climate change on farming. This tone suggests that the author believes the situation is dire and may worsen if not addressed.

distractorRationale.a: An optimistic tone would suggest hope for improvement, which is not present in the passage.
distractorRationale.c: Indifference implies a lack of concern, which contradicts the serious subject matter discussed.
distractorRationale.d: Sarcasm would imply the author is mocking the situation, which is not the case here.
